narrative:
The model determined that you have an 82.3% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence; being in the second decile placed you well below the average student who is admitted. Your first-year ranking in the second decile was the second most important factor and similarly pulled the prediction toward failure. These two performance measures outweighed everything else in the model’s assessment.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.90 was the third most influential piece of information. Although this score worked slightly in your favor compared with the typical admitted student’s 3.23, its positive effect was too small to offset the much stronger negative signals from your class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 31, family income in the upper-middle bracket, full-time study plans, gender, and race played only minor roles and did not meaningfully change the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and class standing in any future coursework, consider retaking the LSAT to reach at least the mid-30s, and then reapply. Demonstrating clear upward progress will be the most effective way to shift future predictions in your favor. (218 words)
